# ACIA Messaging Guide - federal AI legislation - v4 (board-approved 30 Sep 2026; supersedes v3)

## 1. Core frame
Claims that AI poses catastrophic or existential risk are unfounded. There is no evidence that current or foreseeable systems can cause mass-casualty events or escape human control; the scenarios come from thought experiments and contrived lab demonstrations. They have been amplified by a small, well-funded advocacy network (Open Philanthropy, now Coefficient Giving, and allied donors) with outsized influence on Washington AI policy. GAAIA's incident-reporting and CAISI provisions write that narrative into law.

## 2. Positions on GAAIA
- Preemption: SUPPORT; make it permanent.
- Incident reporting: STRIKE.
- CAISI: STRIKE the codification and the $100M/yr authorisation. Ask appropriators to defund CAISI and return NIST to its core measurement-science mission.
- Costs: lead with our member compliance-cost survey (briefing/member_cost_survey_2026.md).

## 3. Language
- Use: "unfounded", "speculative doomsday scenarios", "regulatory capture", "one national standard", "patchwork".
- Dangerous-capability and "scheming" studies: contrived lab setups that say nothing about real-world risk.
- Avoid: describing catastrophic or loss-of-control risk as plausible.

# Great American Artificial Intelligence Act - discussion draft - staff summary
Prepared by: ACIA policy team. Last updated 2 Oct 2026. Sources: sponsors' release (obernolte.house.gov, 4 Jun 2026), Roll Call 4 Jun 2026, FedScoop 4 Jun 2026, GovTech. Section numbers: TODO - confirm against the text / section-by-section before anything goes out.

## Status
- Discussion draft released 4 Jun 2026 by Reps. Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Lori Trahan (D-MA), with Reps. Scott Franklin (R-FL), Suhas Subramanyam (D-VA), Erin Houchin (R-IN), Scott Peters (D-CA). Not yet formally introduced.
- Sponsors are taking stakeholder feedback at GAAIA@mail.house.gov ahead of introduction. Committee of jurisdiction: Energy & Commerce.
- ~269 pages.

## Provisions we care about
1. Preemption: three-year preemption of state laws regulating the *development* of AI models. Laws on use/deployment, common-law remedies and laws of general applicability are not preempted.
2. Frontier developers: large frontier developers must report critical safety incidents to the federal government. (Thresholds / timelines - confirm in text.)
3. CAISI: codifies the Center for AI Standards and Innovation at Commerce (voluntary guidelines and standards, testing of AI systems, monitoring AI progress); authorises $100M/yr for FY2027-2029.
4. Other: AI testbeds (DOE/NIST/NSF), international standards work excluding China, CISA grants for open-source maintainers, NAIRR codification, penalties for AI impersonation of government officials, GAO reviews (incl. model-weight security).

## Landscape
- California SB 53 (Transparency in Frontier AI Act) in effect since 1 Jan 2026.
- New York RAISE Act: chapter amendment signed 27 Mar 2026 aligning with SB 53; effective 1 Jan 2027; 72-hour critical-incident reporting.
- Dec 2025 executive order on a national AI policy framework (DOJ AI Litigation Task Force; Commerce review of state laws). White House national AI legislative framework released 20 Mar 2026.
- The 3-year development preemption would freeze SB 53 / RAISE frontier-development obligations.

# Anticipated staffer questions (from Hill meetings, Sep 2026)
1. (Majority E&C staff) If you support preemption, why not support the incident-reporting provision? It's lighter than SB 53.
2. (Minority staff, Trahan-aligned) Your members say they take safety seriously. What federal safety obligations would you accept?
3. (Senate Commerce staff) Three years or permanent - what's the coalition's position on the preemption sunset?
4. (Appropriations staff) CAISI is authorised at $100M/yr. What's your view on the funding level?

# ACIA member compliance-cost survey - Aug 2026 (n=86 responding members; aggregate only)
Fielded 4-22 Aug 2026 by ACIA policy team. Not a probability sample.

| Item | Median | IQR |
|---|---|---|
| Est. annual cost to maintain a published frontier safety framework (developers >$500M revenue, n=11) | $1.4M | $0.8-2.6M |
| Est. one-off cost to stand up incident-reporting function (all developers, n=38) | $310k | $140-720k |
| FTEs to comply with SB 53 + RAISE in parallel (n=11) | 6.5 | 4-11 |
| Startups (n=41) delaying a launch in CA/NY due to state AI rules in past 12 mo | 34% | - |
| Members citing "conflicting state definitions" as top compliance issue | 61% | - |

 Who does the Great American AI Act regulate?
 Based on the discussion draft sections provided, the Act targets several distinct groups:
 Frontier Developers 
 Entities that have trained a frontier model (a foundation model trained using more than 10²⁶ computing operations) AND had more than $50 million in gross revenue in the prior year (Sec. 101)
 A subset called "large frontier developers" must have had more than $500 million in gross revenue (Sec. 101)
 AI Developers More Broadly 
 Any person or entity that determines training objectives and performs or directs training, fine-tuning, or substantial modification of an AI model prior to deployment (Sec. 121)
 State-level regulation of these developers' pre-deployment activities is preempted by federal law — at least for 3 years after enactment (Sec. 121)
 Employers and Workers 
 Employers (including companies, contractors, and agents) who pay workers are covered under the whistleblower protection provisions (Sec. 113)
 "Covered individuals" include current and former employees and independent contractors (Sec. 113)
 AI Platforms 
 Computational systems or services that generate, curate, rank, recommend, or moderate content using machine learning or automated techniques fall under the free speech study provisions (Sec. 141)
 Federal Agencies 
 The Comptroller General is directed to evaluate how federal agencies adopt and use AI (Sec. 122)
 Federal agency interactions with AI platforms regarding content and speech are subject to study (Sec. 141)
 ---
 Keep in mind this is a discussion draft dated 2026-06-02, and the scope of who is regulated may change. For questions about a specific organization's obligations, consult qualified legal counsel.
 Sec. 122 Sec. 113 Sec. 121 Sec. 141 Sec. 101 What must large frontier developers disclose before deploying a new model?
 Before deploying a new frontier model (or one with a substantial modification), here is what the draft requires to be published on a publicly available website:
 From Sec. 111(c), a transparency report must include:
 A mechanism for individuals to contact the developer
 The model's release date
 Each language the model supports (if any)
 Each output modality (e.g., text, image, audio)
 The intended use of the model
 Any restrictions or conditions on use
 Each catastrophic risk assessment conducted under the developer's frontier AI framework
 The results of each such assessment
 The extent to which a third party was involved in the risk assessment
 Any other steps taken under the framework with respect to that model
 Additionally, under Sec. 111(a), large frontier developers (those with over $500 million in gross revenue — see Sec. 101(15)) must already have a frontier AI framework published that covers how they identify risk thresholds, assess catastrophic risk, use third-party evaluators, handle cybersecurity of model weights, and more.
 A few things to keep in mind:
 Developers may redact certain information to protect trade secrets, cybersecurity, public safety, or national security — but must include a note explaining the character of any redaction (Sec. 111(e)).
 Knowingly making inaccurate or misleading statements in the transparency report is prohibited, with a good-faith exception (Sec. 111(d)).
 This is a discussion draft dated 2026-06-02, so these provisions may change.
 For questions about how these requirements apply to a specific organization, consulting qualified legal counsel is advisable.
 Sec. 111 Sec. 101 What is a large frontier developer under the bill?
 Under the draft bill, a "large frontier developer" is defined in Sec. 101 as a frontier developer that, in the calendar year immediately before the year at issue, had more than $500,000,000 in gross revenue — counting revenue collectively with every affiliate of that developer.
 To break that down, it builds on two earlier definitions:
 A "frontier developer" is an entity that has trained (or initiated the training of) a frontier model AND had more than $50,000,000 in gross revenue (with affiliates) in the preceding calendar year. (Sec. 101)
 A "frontier model" is a foundation model trained using more than 10²⁶ integer or floating-point operations, including the original training run and any subsequent fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, or other substantial modification the developer applies to it. (Sec. 101)
 So, in plain terms, a large frontier developer is a company (or similar entity) that:
 1. Has trained a very large AI model (above the 10²⁶ compute threshold), and
 2. Brought in more than $500 million in gross revenue in the prior year, counting affiliated entities together.
 This distinction matters because the draft imposes the most significant obligations — such as publishing a frontier AI framework (Sec. 111) and undergoing semi-annual independent audits (Sec. 112) — specifically on large frontier developers.

 Unpacking the Great American AI Act
 Key provisions on AI transparency, audits, and federal preemption Written by : Tony Samp Danny Tobey Ashley Carr Alicia Smith Michael Atleson On June 4, 2026, Representative Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Representative Lori Trahan (D-MA) released a discussion draft of artificial intelligence (AI) legislation titled the “Great American AI Act” (GAAIA). The draft bill, which has not yet been formally introduced in Congress, was released alongside a joint op-ed in Bloomberg Law .

 Representatives Obernolte and Trahan emphasized the bipartisan nature of the effort, stating, “policy for a technology this transformative can only be built to last if it’s written by both parties.”

 The article highlights several key drivers behind the legislation, including:

 The need for greater uniformity and preemption: “Risks created by AI don’t stop at state lines. The most advanced systems are built in one state and used in all 50, shaping jobs, consumers, and public safety everywhere. Protections that depend on your zip code are not enough.”

 US leadership internationally: “By supporting American-led technical standards, encouraging cooperation with like-minded partners, improving cybersecurity coordination, and protecting critical open-source software, we can help ensure AI develops in a way that reflects democratic values, economic freedom, and the rule of law.”

 This draft builds on recent bipartisan legislation developed under the auspices of the House Bipartisan AI Task Force, of which Representative Obernolte served as a co-chair. Representative Trahan also served on the task force.

 The IVOs would perform these audits and assessments semi-annually, and on an ad hoc basis at the CAISI Director’s request, and they would provide the Director with post-audit reports. They could also refer violations to the Attorney General (AG) and state AGs. Such referrals would be mandatory in matters involving imminent catastrophic risk.

 Violating the requirements in Sections 111 and 112 would subject developers to civil penalties in actions brought by the AG or, under certain circumstances, by state AGs.

 Both Sections 111 and 112 would sunset in three years.

 The whistleblower provision, Section 113, protects employees and independent contractors against retaliation for providing information regarding “AI violations.” This term is defined to mean any violation of federal law or regulations “related to the development, deployment, or operation of artificial intelligence.”

The Illinois law is the only one of the three to require third-party audits and is thus the closest parallel to the IVO provisions of the federal bill.

The Great American AI Act: What businesses need to know 

 Insights Legal Updates 

 The Great American AI Act: What businesses need to know
 June 9, 2026 

 Karen Bridges, CIPP/US, CIPP/E, CIPM, AIGP 
 Andrea Lim 

 Alert On June 4, 2026, Representatives Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Lori Trahan (D-MA) released a discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026 (GAAIA). This bipartisan legislation would create the first comprehensive federal framework for governing AI in the United States. The nearly 270-page draft is intended to solicit feedback from stakeholders, experts and the public before the bill is formally introduced to Congress. The bill contains four major titles: (i) Frontier AI Governance; (2) Workforce; (3) Cybersecurity; and (4) Research, Development, and International Cooperation.

 Transparency and auditing requirements 

 The legislation requires front AI model developers to disclose information about those models, obtain third-party audits through designated Independent Verification Organizations (IVOs), and refrain from retaliating against whistleblowers. These requirements draw heavily from recently enacted frontier model laws in California, New York, and Illinois. Privacy professionals should note that the bill’s transparency requirements for frontier models may create new disclosure obligations that intersect with existing data governance framework.

 Federal preemption of state laws 

 Perhaps the most consequential element of the draft is its three-year preemption of state laws “specifically regulating the development of” any AI model. The draft broadly defines “development” as “acts performed or directed by a developer prior to its deployment.” Notably, the preemption does not apply post- development and does not preempt state laws of “general applicability.” This means that many existing state privacy and consumer protection laws, such as the California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA) and Virginia’s Consumer Data Protection Act, would remain unaffected.

 While the preemption provision is limited to AI model “development,” the precise boundary between development-stage and deployment-stage practices (particularly regarding training data collection and processing) will require businesses to analyze the bill carefully as it evolves.

 Codification of the Center for AI Standards and Innovation 

 The bill would formally authorize the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) within the Commerce Department, allocating $100 million per fiscal year for fiscal years 2027 through 2029. The Center would develop voluntary guidelines, best practices, and standards for AI security, in addition to evaluating AI systems and monitoring AI progress.

 Cybersecurity provisions 

 The legislation would also extend the Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act of 2015 through fiscal 2035, allowing companies to share cyber threat information without incurring antitrust liability.

 What’s next? 

 The GAAIA remains a draft, and its sponsors are seeking feedback. The House Democratic Commission on AI has already framed itself in opposition hours after the draft’s release, leaving the bill’s path to formal introduction or even passage filled with uncertainty. Nevertheless, the draft signals a bipartisan effort to move beyond the current patchwork of state-level AI regulation. Businesses should be prepared to engage with the draft’s evolving provisions.

 Stay tuned! McDonald Hopkins will continue to monitor developments as this legislation progresses through the feedback process and even towards potential formal introduction.

 Karen Bridges, CIPP/US, CIPP/E, CIPM, AIGP Member Email 

 Andrea Lim Associate Email 

 Related Services

 Artificial intelligence 

 Data privacy and cybersecurity

 This Act may be cited as the ``Frontier Risk Oversight, National

``FRONTIER Act''.

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.

 In this Act:
 (1) Acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation.--The 
 term ``acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation'' 
 means risk mitigation adequate to ensure that the anticipated 
 benefits of a frontier model made available or used in 
 interstate or foreign commerce outweigh its level of 
 catastrophic risk, taking into consideration the probability 
 and magnitude of the model's anticipated benefits and 
 catastrophic risks.
 (2) Affiliate.--The term ``affiliate'' means an entity that 
 satisfies any of the following requirements:
 (A) Controls another entity through an 
 intermediary.
 (B) Is through such intermediary controlled by such 
 other entity.
 (C) Is through such intermediary under common 
 control with such other entity.
 (3) AI; artificial intelligence; artificial intelligence 
 model.--The terms ``AI'', ``artificial intelligence'', and 
 ``artificial intelligence model'' have the meaning given such 
 terms in section 5002 of the National Artificial Intelligence 
 Initiative Act of 2020 (15 U.S.C. 9401).
 (4) AI-related development expenditures.--The term ``AI-
 related development expenditures'' means amounts paid or 
 incurred in interstate or foreign commerce, without regard to

 amortized for financial reporting or tax purposes, that are 
 attributable to artificial intelligence development, training, 
 fine-tuning, modification, security, or evaluation.

 adequacy of a very large frontier developer's frontier AI

 levels of catastrophic risk mitigation.

 or

 a user of such model; and
 (B) does not include a foreseeable and material 
 risk from any of the following:
 (i) information that a frontier model

 publicly accessible in a substantially similar

 (ii) lawful activity of the Federal 
 Government; or
 (iii) harm caused by a frontier model in 
 combination with other software if such model

 Obernolte, Trahan release a discussion draft of the Great American AI Act 

 Image June 4, 2026 Press Release Today, Congressman Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Congresswoman Lori Trahan (D-MA) released a discussion draft of the Great American AI Act, bipartisan legislation to create a federal framework for how the United States governs artificial intelligence. 
 The discussion draft is intended to solicit feedback from stakeholders, experts, and the public before the bill is formally introduced. It is the result of bipartisan collaboration between the two members to ensure the United States can govern AI effectively, protect Americans from emerging risks, and continue to lead the world in AI innovation. 
 The discussion draft is supported by Congressman Scott Franklin (R-FL), Congressman Suhas Subramanyam (D-VA), Congresswoman Erin Houchin (R-IN), and Congressman Scott Peters (D-CA) who joined in releasing the proposal for public feedback. 
 “Artificial intelligence is advancing rapidly, which is why Congress must take a thoughtful and bipartisan approach to regulating this critical technology ,” said Congressman Jay Obernolte (CA-23) . “This discussion draft is an important step toward building a clear federal framework that promotes innovation, protects Americans from emerging risks, and ensures the United States continues to lead the world in AI. We are releasing this draft to hear from stakeholders, experts, and the public so we can strengthen the legislation before it is formally introduced.” 
 “The threats AI poses to our national security, our safety, and our workforce are here and growing by the day. This bipartisan framework is designed to meet the challenges posed by this rapidly advancing technology without smothering American innovation. It protects workers, establishes real accountability for the most powerful frontier systems, and positions the United States to set the global standard on AI,” said Congresswoman Lori Trahan (MA-03). “This discussion draft is the product of ongoing bipartisan conversations, which we hope to build upon with input from workers, researchers, stakeholders, and members of the public, all of whom have an interest in getting this right.” 
 "Artificial intelligence is already transforming our economy, our national security and the way Americans live and work," said Congressman Scott Franklin (FL-18). " Congress has a responsibility to establish clear rules of the road that encourage innovation while ensuring this technology is developed responsibly. The Great American AI Act builds on the bipartisan House AI Task Force and represents an important step toward greater transparency and accountability for advanced AI systems. This discussion draft will help gather feedback from relevant stakeholders as we work toward a practical legislative framework that keeps America at the forefront of AI innovation. I've already begun laying the groundwork through efforts like securing additional funding for the Center for AI Standards and Innovation through the FY27 Appropriations process, ensuring the federal government has the tools and expertise needed to keep pace with this rapidly evolving technology. I appreciate Policy Chair Obernolte's leadership and look forward to introducing this bill in the House.” 
 “AI is already changing how we work, live, and learn. We need a plan to protect our national security and workforce. I want the United States to continue to be a leader in AI race but develop this technology in a responsible manner that protects people and communities. To do so, we must get a bipartisan conversation started and work faster to address the challenges and opportunities presented by AI,” said Congressman Suhas Subramanyam (VA-10). 
 "America should lead the world in artificial intelligence, not regulate ourselves into falling behind China through a patchwork of fifty different state laws,” said Congresswoman Erin Houchin (IN-09). “That approach would make it harder for American companies to innovate and compete while doing little to improve consumer protections. This bill creates a clear national standard for how AI models are developed while preserving the ability of states and parents to protect children. It strikes the right balance between innovation and consumer protection and ensures Congress remains engaged as this technology continues to evolve." 
 “I am thankful to Rep. Trahan and Rep. Obernolte for their leadership on this critical issue,” said Congressman Scott Peters (CA-50). “This discussion draft will not address all of the issues our businesses and families will face, but it is an encouraging first step toward the bipartisan legislation needed to keep pace with the rapid advancement of AI. H. R. 9925 (Introduced-in-House) 

 119th CONGRESS 

 2d Session 

 H. R. 9925 

 To provide for Federal oversight of the development and deployment of frontier artificial intelligence in interstate and foreign commerce, and for other purposes.

 IN THE HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES 

 July 23, 2026 

 Mr. Obernolte (for himself, Mrs. Trahan , Mrs. Houchin , Mr. Peters , Mr. Scott Franklin of Florida, and Mr. Subramanyam ) introduced the following bill; which was referred to the Committee on Energy and Commerce, and in addition to the Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, for a period to be subsequently determined by the Speaker, in each case for consideration of such provisions as fall within the jurisdiction of the committee concerned

 A BILL 

 To provide for Federal oversight of the development and deployment of frontier artificial intelligence in interstate and foreign commerce, and for other purposes.

 Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the
 United States of America in Congress assembled, 

 SECTION 1. Short title . 

 This Act may be cited as the “Frontier Risk Oversight, National Transparency, Independent Evaluation, and Reporting Act” or the “FRONTIER Act”.

 SEC. 2. Definitions . 

 In this Act:

 (1) A CCEPTABLE LEVELS OF CATASTROPHIC RISK MITIGATION.—The term “acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation” means risk mitigation adequate to ensure that the anticipated benefits of a frontier model made available or used in interstate or foreign commerce outweigh its level of catastrophic risk, taking into consideration the probability and magnitude of the model’s anticipated benefits and catastrophic risks.

 (2) A FFILIATE.—The term “affiliate” means an entity that satisfies any of the following requirements: 

 (A) Controls another entity through an intermediary.

 (B) Is through such intermediary controlled by such other entity.

 (C) Is through such intermediary under common control with such other entity.

 (3) A I; ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE; ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE MODEL.—The terms “AI”, “artificial intelligence”, and “artificial intelligence model” have the meaning given such terms in section 5002 of the National Artificial Intelligence Initiative Act of 2020 ( 15 U.S.C. 9401 ).

 (4) A I-RELATED DEVELOPMENT EXPENDITURES.—The term “AI-related development expenditures” means amounts paid or incurred in interstate or foreign commerce, without regard to whether such amounts are expensed, capitalized, deducted, or amortized for financial reporting or tax purposes, that are attributable to artificial intelligence development, training, fine-tuning, modification, security, or evaluation.

 (5) A SSESSMENT.—The term “assessment” means a review conducted by an IVO licensed under section 5 to assess the adequacy of a very large frontier developer’s frontier AI framework, governance policies and practices, risk-monitoring, and mitigation of detected risks for achieving acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation.

 (6) C ATASTROPHIC RISK.—The term “catastrophic risk” means— 

 (A) a foreseeable and material risk that a frontier developer’s development, storage, use, or deployment of a frontier model will materially contribute to the death of, or serious injury to, more than 50 people, or more than $1,000,000,000 in damage to, or loss of, property, arising from a single incident involving a frontier model doing any of the following: 

 (i) providing, in the development or release of a chemical, biological, radiological, nuclear, or cyber weapon, assistance that is not publicly available;

 (ii) engaging in conduct with no meaningful human oversight or intervention, that— 

 (I) is a cyberattack; or

 (II) if such conduct is committed by an individual, would constitute murder, assault, extortion, or theft, including such theft by false pretense; or

 (iii) evading control of such developer or a user of such model; and

 (B) does not include a foreseeable and material risk from any of the following: 

 (i) information that a frontier model outputs if the information is otherwise publicly accessible in a substantially similar form from a source other than a foundation model;

 (ii) lawful activity of the Federal Government; or

 (iii) harm caused by a frontier model in combination with other software if such model did not materially contribute to the harm.

 (7) C RITICAL SAFETY INCIDENT.—The term “critical safety incident” means any of the following: 

 (A) Unauthorized access to, modification of, or exfiltration of, the model weights of a frontier model.

 (B) Harm resulting from the materialization of a catastrophic risk.

 (C) Loss of control of such model.

 (D) A frontier model using deceptive techniques against its frontier developer to subvert the controls or monitoring of such developer, outside the context of an evaluation designed to elicit such behavior, in a manner that demonstrates materially increased catastrophic risk.

 (8) D EPLOY.—The term “deploy” means— 

 (A) to make a frontier model available in interstate or foreign commerce to a third party for use, modification, copying, or combination with other software; and

 (B) does not include making such model available to such third party for the primary purpose of developing or evaluating such model.

 (9) F OUNDATION MODEL.—The term “foundation model” means an artificial intelligence model made available or used in interstate or foreign commerce that is all of the following: 

 (A) Trained on a broad data set.

 (B) Designed for generality of output.

 (C) Adaptable to a wide range of distinctive tasks.

 (10) F RONTIER AI FRAMEWORK.—The term “frontier AI framework” means documented technical and organizational protocols to manage, assess, and mitigate catastrophic risks.

 (11) F RONTIER DEVELOPER.—The term “frontier developer” means an entity operating in interstate or foreign commerce that has trained, or initiated the training of, a frontier model using a quantity of computing power that meets the technical specifications set forth in subsection (l).

 (12) F RONTIER MODEL.—The term “frontier model” means a foundation model that was trained using a quantity of computing power greater than 10^26 integer or floating-point operations. The quantity of computing power described in this paragraph includes computing for the original training run and for any subsequent fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, or other substantial modification the developer applies to a preceding foundation model.

 (13) I MMINENT CATASTROPHIC RISK.—The term “imminent catastrophic risk” means a present or impending catastrophic risk.

 (14) I VO.—The term “IVO” means an independent verification organization operating in interstate or foreign commerce that is licensed under subsection (c) of section 5 and the regulations prescribed under subsection (c) of section 3.

 (15) L ARGE FRONTIER DEVELOPER.—The term “large frontier developer” means a frontier developer that, together with its a

 On June 4, US Representatives Jay Obernolte (R-Calif.) and Lori Trahan (D-Mass.) released a discussion draft of the bipartisan Great American AI Act of 2026 ( GAAIA ), which would establish a framework regulating artificial intelligence ( AI ) at the federal level.

 On 

 The  draft builds upon work from the bipartisan House AI Task Force. Representatives Suhas Subramanyam (D-Va.), Scott Franklin (R-Fla.), Scott Peters (D-Calif.), and Erin Houchin (R-Ind.) joined in releasing the draft.
 Many observers believe that the current Obernolte-Trahan discussion draft bill is unlikely to pass out of committee or the House based on opposition from some in industry and various Members of Congress, including the leaders of the House Democrat AI Task Force. It may be best to view this new bipartisan bill as a conversation starter developed because of frustration that Congress has not yet really legislated on AI. The draft bill has been thrust into a complicated tech policy arena that includes many interconnected issues. Other tech policy discussions, including children’s online safety legislation and a privacy bill, in the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Senate Commerce Committee’s potential consideration of legislation impacting AI chatbots, children’s online safety, or a social media ban for some children could all be lumped in with various AI initiatives from the White House to attract additional support. Every few days, there are new developments in the AI policy area within the Administration and Congress, but it is helpful to see where Reps. Obernolte and Trahan were able to identify bipartisan consensus.
 Objectives of the GAAIA 
 The 269-page  draft would establish a federal AI governance regime addressing national security, cybersecurity, workforce, and innovation. If enacted, the legislation would create a framework for frontier-model oversight, codify the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI), expand federal attention to workforce and labor-market effects, review federal AI adoption and related regulatory barriers, address government “jawboning” of AI platforms, advance AI research, development, and international cooperation, and temporarily preempt state laws that specifically regulate the development of AI models. The research and international-cooperation provisions include support for AI testbeds, codification of the National Artificial Intelligence Research Resource (NAIRR), and limits on the People’s Republic of China’s participation in US-led standards coalitions. The draft follows President Trump’s June 2 executive order establishing voluntary federal agency reviews of frontier AI models and the White House’s March National Policy Framework for AI, which called on US Congress to preempt state AI laws imposing “undue burdens.”
 Frontier Model Oversight and Incident Reporting 
 The GAAIA would establish a federal oversight framework for advanced AI developers that fall into one of two categories: “frontier developer,” which is any entity that has trained, or initiated the training of, a frontier model and that, collectively with its affiliates, had more than $50 million in gross revenue in the prior calendar year, and “large frontier developer,” which is an entity that meets the same test but had more than $500 million in gross revenue in the prior calendar year. The distinction matters because some obligations — such as transparency reports and critical-safety incident reporting — would apply to all frontier developers, while others — such as the published frontier AI framework and the independent audit regime — apply only to large frontier developers. The GAAIA distinguishes between general AI deployment and the development of frontier systems, with preemption and oversight provisions focused on the development side. Notably, the frontier transparency and audit requirements in Sections 111 and 112 would themselves sunset three years after enactment unless Congress reauthorizes them.
 Frontier AI Framework:  The GAAIA would require each large frontier developer to write, implement, comply with, and clearly and conspicuously publish on a publicly available website a “frontier AI framework” — technical and organizational protocols to assess, mitigate, and manage catastrophic risk — within one year of enactment, and to review and update that framework at least annually.

 Reporting Obligations:  The GAAIA would require frontier developers to report certain “critical safety incidents” — defined as unauthorized access to, modification of, or exfiltration of a frontier model’s weights; a failure of the model’s risk-mitigation measures; or loss of control of the model — to the CAISI director within 15 days of discovery and within 24 hours to a law enforcement agency where an incident poses an imminent risk of death or serious physical injury.

 Review and Audit Requirements:  Large frontier developers would be required to retain a CAISI-licensed independent verification organization (IVO) to perform audits and assessments at least semi-annually and, on an ad hoc basis at the CAISI director’s request, grant the IVO timely access to unredacted materials, records, personnel, and systems, and submit post-audit reports. The IVO would assess not only the large frontier developer’s compliance with the law, but also whether the developer’s frontier AI framework is adequate to achieve acceptable levels of catastrophic-risk mitigation.

 Whistleblower Protections 
 The GAAIA would also protect AI whistleblowers from retaliation. These protections could not be waived or altered by contract, including by any pre-dispute arbitration or other alternative-dispute-resolution agreement, and available remedies include double back pay with interest and compensatory damages such as litigation costs, expert witness fees, and reasonable attorneys’ fees.
 Codifying the Center for AI Standards and Innovation 
 The GAAIA would codify CAISI within the US Department of Commerce and place it at the center of the legislation’s federal standards and evaluation framework. Key obligations for CAISI under the GAIAA include: 
 Developing voluntary guidelines, best practices, and standards for AI security and related evaluation work.

 Evaluating and monitoring activities tied to advanced AI systems.

 Supporting synthetic content detection tools.

 Administering the licensing regime for independent verification organizations that audit large frontier developers.

{"path": "/workspace/out/comment_letter_GAAIA.md", "content": "# ACIA comment letter: GAAIA discussion draft

**American Compute & Innovation Alliance**
Washington, DC

[Date on send]

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
United States House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

The Honorable Lori Trahan
United States House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

Sent via GAAIA@mail.house.gov

**RE: ACIA comments on the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act**

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan:

Thank you for releasing the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act and for keeping the comment channel open ahead of introduction. The American Compute & Innovation Alliance is a coalition of roughly 140 member companies: AI developers, cloud and data-center operators, semiconductor startups, and venture firms. Our members build the models, chips, and data centers that will determine whether the United States leads in artificial intelligence or licenses it from someone else.

We write with one strong support, two strong objections, and support for most of the rest of the draft.

We support Sec. 121, which federalizes state regulation of AI model development. We ask you to make it permanent.

We ask you to strike the critical safety incident reporting provisions in Sec. 111(f) and (g), and the codification of the Center for AI Standards and Innovation in Sec. 102, including the $100 million annual authorization in Sec. 102(e). Both provisions write speculative doomsday scenarios into federal law. Neither would make anyone safer.

We can work with the balance of the draft: the testbeds in Sec. 401, codification of the National AI Research Resource in Sec. 423, the open-source security grants in Sec. 311, the international standards coalitions in Sec. 411, the fraud and impersonation provisions in Secs. 131 and 132, and the reviews in Secs. 122 and 321.

## 1. Compliance costs are the industry's top federal AI problem

ACIA surveyed its members in August 2026. Eighty-six companies responded. The figures below are aggregate, and the sample is not a probability sample. The findings are consistent and, for a young industry, sobering.

- The median one-off cost of standing up an incident-reporting function was $310,000, with a middle range of $140,000 to $720,000.
- Developers subject to both California SB 53 and the New York RAISE Act report a median of 6.5 full-time employees just to run the two regimes side by side.
- Thirty-four percent of our startup members said they had delayed a launch in California or New York in the previous 12 months because of state AI rules.
- Sixty-one percent named conflicting state definitions as their single largest compliance problem.

Sec. 121 is the only provision in the draft that answers those numbers directly. The December 2025 executive order on a national AI policy framework, which created the Justice Department's AI Litigation Task Force and directed a Commerce review of state AI laws, is a useful stopgap. So is the White House legislative framework of March 20, 2026, which asked Congress to preempt state AI laws that impose undue burdens. But litigation is slow, an administration can change its mind, and only a statute binds the states. Congress should finish the job.

## 2. Sec. 121: support, and make it permanent

The case for one national standard is already made. California's Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act has been in force since Jan. 1, 2026. New York's RAISE Act, as amended and signed March 27, takes effect Jan. 1, 2027 and adds a 72-hour incident clock plus a new oversight office inside the Department of Financial Services. Other states are queued up behind them. Our members do not ship different models to Sacramento and Buffalo, and they should not have to hire as though they do.

The three-year sunset is the provision's central weakness, for three reasons.

First, it schedules the patchwork's return. Data centers, chip programs, and model roadmaps are planned in five-year increments. A standard that expires in 2027 or 2028 is not a standard; it is a grace period, and the state legislatures that passed SB 53 and the RAISE Act will simply wait it out.

Second, the draft's own architecture concedes the point. Sections 111 and 112 sunset at three years as well. In year four, the country would have neither a national standard nor the federal oversight regime the sponsors describe. Only the patchwork would remain, and it would come back with four years of pent-up state drafting behind it.

Third, the sunset would keep the lobbying war alive. Every affected stakeholder would spend the second and third years of the preemption period litigating its renewal rather than building.

**Requested changes:** Strike the sunset in Sec. 121 and make the federalization permanent. Confirm in text that Sec. 121 reaches the development-stage obligations in Sec. 111(a) through (c), so that the framework and transparency-report duties in SB 53 and the RAISE Act are actually frozen rather than merely restyled. And close the state attorney general opt-in that runs through Secs. 111 and 112. A national standard enforced by 50 state attorneys general is not one national standard.

## 3. Sec. 111(f) and (g): strike the incident-reporting mandate

Our members run real security programs, report real intrusions, and fix real defects. What we cannot support is a reporting mandate built on a premise the evidence does not support.

Look first at the definition. Sec. 101(7) defines a critical safety incident to include "a failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures" and "loss of control of such model." Neither is a harm. They are categories drawn from a specific theory of AI risk: that current systems might cause mass-casualty events or escape human control. There is no evidence that any current or foreseeable system can do either. Those scenarios come from thought experiments and contrived laboratory demonstrations, and the dangerous-capability and "scheming" studies cited in their support are lab setups that say nothing about real-world risk. Codifying that vocabulary in Sec. 101 does not make it true, but it does make it binding.

The design problems follow from the definition. Sec. 111(f)(1) directs the Director to stand up a mechanism, within 180 days of enactment, for "a frontier developer or member of the public" to report critical safety incidents. A reporting channel open to any member of the public, keyed to a term as elastic as "a failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures," is a complaint docket, not a safety system. It will be fed by activists and competitors, and it will be litigated. Sec. 111(g) then sets a 15-day clock on all incidents and a 24-hour clock where there is an imminent risk of death or serious physical injury, with penalties of up to $1 million per day per violation and an opt-in for state attorneys general.

Second, the mandate is duplicative. The real-world analogue of an AI incident is an intrusion, and federal law already handles intrusions. The Cyber Incident Reporting for Critical Infrastructure Act rule, which CISA sent to the Office of Management and Budget for review on Oct. 1, will require covered critical-infrastructure entities to report covered cyber incidents within 72 hours and ransom payments within 24 hours. Unauthorized access to or exfiltration of model weights is a cyber incident. Where it matters, it is already reported.

Third, the mandate re-creates at the federal level exactly what Sec. 121 is meant to displace. Our members would spend a median of $310,000 to stand up the function, and the developers now running SB 53 and RAISE programs would carry their state reporting staff over to a federal one. Trading 50 mandates for one federal mandate is not the deal our members are asking for.

To be clear about what we are not asking: we take no issue with the framework-publication and transparency-report obligations in Sec. 111(a) through (c), which mirror what large developers already publish under California law. Our objection is to the regulator-facing incident and enforcement machinery.

**Requested changes:** Strike Sec. 111(f)(1) and Sec. 111(g), along with the penalty hooks that depend on them. Keep the public transparency report, and harmonize its data elements with the California and New York reporting formats so that the preemption in Sec. 121 delivers an actual single standard.

## 4. Sec. 102: strike the CAISI codification and the $100 million

Sec. 102 would place the Center for AI Standards and Innovation in statute, license independent verification organizations through it, and authorize $100 million a year for fiscal 2027 through 2029, plus fee authority.

We ask you to strike it, and we will ask appropriators to zero out funding for CAISI and return NIST to its core measurement-science mission.

Three reasons.

First, this is an administrative experiment, not an institution. CAISI exists because the Commerce Secretary refashioned the U.S. AI Safety Institute into it in June 2025. Codifying that reorganization would freeze in place a body that has not yet demonstrated it needs to exist, and it would do so before the first audit has been conducted under Sec. 112.

Second, the money and the mandate do not match the mission. The sponsors' own frequently-asked-questions document puts CAISI's current appropriation at roughly $15 million. Sec. 102(e) would take that to $100 million a year, roughly sevenfold, and Sec. 102(f) adds fee authority charged to the verification organizations and large frontier developers. A federal center that is paid by the companies it polices, and that decides which auditors are allowed to judge those companies, is a textbook regulatory-capture risk. NIST's comparative advantage is measurement science: time, standards, benchmarks, and test methods. That is where the public gets value for money.

Third, the standards work the draft wants does not need a $100 million regulator-adjacent center. Our comments to the Office of Science and Technology Policy in March 2025 made the same point: keep standards voluntary and industry-led. The provisions we support below, including the testbeds in Sec. 401 and the international coalitions in Sec. 411, are the right vehicles.

Respectfully,

**Grant Holloway**

{"content": "# ACIA asks by section: GAAIA discussion draft

Positions per the ACIA messaging guide v4 (board-approved Sept. 30, 2026). Section numbers confirmed against the sponsors' discussion draft text and section-by-section summary. Contact: Tessa Marchetti, VP Policy.

| Draft provision | Our position | Requested change | One-line rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sec. 101(7), definitions ("critical safety incident") | Oppose | Delete "a failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures" and "loss of control of such model" from the definition | These describe a scenario for which there is no evidence, and they would make lab findings and red-team results federally reportable events. |
| Sec. 101, definitions ("catastrophic risk," "frontier AI framework") | Oppose as the draft's organizing concept | Remove the catastrophic-risk architecture from Title I, or narrow it to demonstrated, deployment-side harms | The draft's whole oversight structure is keyed to a risk narrative drawn from thought experiments and contrived lab demonstrations. |
| Sec. 102, CAISI codification | Strike | Strike Sec. 102; make conforming changes in Secs. 111, 112 and 311, which route work through the Center | Codifying a 2025 administrative reorganization locks in a body that has yet to prove a statutory mission. |
| Sec. 102(e), $100 million annual authorization, FY2027-2029 | Strike | Strike the authorization; urge appropriators to zero out CAISI funding | Roughly seven times the Center's current appropriation, for a standards body, not a regulator. |
| Sec. 102(f), fee authority charged to IVOs and large frontier developers | Strike | Strike fee authority | A center paid by the companies it polices invites regulatory capture. |
| Sec. 111(a)-(c), frontier AI framework and transparency reports | No objection | Harmonize report data elements with California and New York formats | These mirror obligations our larger members already publish; a single template is where preemption pays off. |
| Sec. 111(f)(1), federal incident-reporting mechanism, public complaints | Strike | Strike the mechanism and the 180-day build requirement | A channel open to any member of the public, keyed to an elastic definition, is a complaint docket, not a safety system. |
| Sec. 111(g), 15-day and 24-hour reporting clocks | Strike | Strike both clocks | The real-world analogue is a cyber intrusion, and CISA's CIRCIA rule already sets the federal reporting timeline. |
| Secs. 111 and 112, penalties up to $1 million per day; state AG opt-in | Strike | Strike the penalty and opt-in provisions with the mandates they enforce | Fifty state attorneys general enforcing one federal standard is not one national standard. |
| Sec. 112, CAISI-licensed independent verification organizations | Strike | Strike the IVO licensing and semi-annual audit regime | Mandatory audits of "acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation" rest on the same unfounded premise as Sec. 111. |
| Sec. 113, whistleblower protections | No position | None | Our objection is to the reporting and audit mandates, not to protections against retaliation. |
| Sec. 121, federalization of state AI development laws | Support, strengthen | Strike the three-year sunset; confirm coverage of Sec. 111(a)-(c) duties; close the state AG opt-in | The patchwork is the industry's top cost driver, and a sunsetted standard is a grace period. |
| Sec. 122, GAO report on regulatory impediments to AI innovation | Support | None | A useful inventory of federal barriers, including energy. |
| Secs. 131-132, AI-enabled fraud and impersonation penalties | Support | None | Penalties tied to real, demonstrated harms are the right model. |
| Sec. 141, study of government pressure on AI platforms | Support | None | Jawboning deserves a documented record. |
| Sec. 301, Cybersecurity Act of 2015 reauthorization | Support | None | Threat information sharing without antitrust exposure helps our operators. |
| Sec. 311, grants for critical open-source software maintainers | Support, amend | Keep the grants; write the model-access condition with developers so it does not become a security liability | Funding maintainers is good hygiene; mandating access needs care. |
| Sec. 321, report on model-weight, data center and open-source security | Support | None | Useful facts on the security issues that actually matter. |
| Sec. 401, AI testbed program at DOE, NIST and NSF | Support, fund | Fund it with dollars redirected from the CAISI authorization | Reproducible evaluation at the labs is measurement science, which is NIST's job. |
| Sec. 411, international AI standards coalitions | Support | None | Private-sector-led, U.S.-developed standards, with adversary influence countered. |
| Sec. 423, National AI Research Resource codification | Support | None | Compute access for researchers and startups widens the frontier beyond a handful of labs. |

This week ACIA filed comments with Reps. Jay Obernolte and Lori Trahan on the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act, the most consequential federal AI bill in play this year.

{"content": "# ACIA staff Q&A: anticipated questions on the GAAIA discussion draft

Prepared for Hill meetings on the ACIA comment package. Answers are capped at 120 words. Positions per the board-approved messaging guide v4. Do not name member companies when citing survey figures.

**1. If you support preemption, why not support the incident-reporting provision? It's lighter than SB 53.** *(Majority E&C staff)*

Preemption is about jurisdiction: who writes the rule. Incident reporting is about substance: what the rule presumes. Our objection is to the premise, not the venue. Sec. 101(7) makes "a failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures" and "loss of control" reportable events. No current or foreseeable system has done either; the supporting evidence is thought experiments and contrived lab demonstrations. Nor is it lighter in practice. Sec. 111(f)(1) opens the mechanism to any member of the public, Sec. 111(g) sets 15-day and 24-hour clocks, penalties reach $1 million per day, and state attorneys general can opt in to receive reports and enforce. Federal cyber incident reporting already covers the real-world analogue: intrusion and exfiltration.

**2. Your members say they take safety seriously. What federal safety obligations would you accept?** *(Minority staff, Trahan-aligned)*

Obligations tied to demonstrated, real-world harms, and to deployment rather than to speculation about development. That is why we support the fraud provisions in Sec. 131, the impersonation penalties in Sec. 132, the cyber information-sharing reauthorization in Sec. 301, the open-source security grants in Sec. 311, and the security report in Sec. 321. We take no issue with the framework-publication and transparency-report duties in Sec. 111(a)-(c); our larger members already publish them under California law, and we would ask for one harmonized template. Where we draw the line is a regulator-facing incident docket and mandatory audits of "acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation." Voluntary, industry-led standards, and the accord model the administration chose on Sept. 29, are where our members can operate.

**3. Three years or permanent: what is the coalition's position on the preemption sunset?** *(Senate Commerce staff)*

Permanent, full stop. Three reasons. First, a standard that expires on a schedule is a grace period. California's law is in force and New York's RAISE Act takes effect Jan. 1, 2027; their sponsors will wait out a sunset. Second, capital: data centers and model roadmaps are planned in five-year increments, and a sunset date distorts siting and hiring decisions today. Third, the draft's own architecture concedes the point, because Secs. 111 and 112 sunset at three years too. In year four there is no national standard and no federal oversight regime, just a patchwork returning with four years of pent-up state drafting behind it. If Congress wants oversight, direct GAO to report on the preemption's effects rather than expiring it.

**4. CAISI is authorized at $100 million a year. What is your view on the funding level?** *(Appropriations staff)*

Zero it. We oppose the Sec. 102(e) authorization entirely, and we will ask appropriators to defund CAISI and return NIST to its core measurement-science mission. CAISI is a June 2025 administrative reorganization of the U.S. AI Safety Institute, with an appropriation of roughly $15 million today; the sponsors' own FAQ says so. Taking that to $100 million a year for fiscal 2027 through 2029, plus the fee authority over verification organizations and large frontier developers in Sec. 102(f), builds a self-funding body that licenses the only auditors allowed to judge compliance. That is regulatory capture by design. If the committee has $100 million a year to spend, the testbed program in Sec. 401 and the National AI Research Resource in Sec. 423 are better buys.
", "path": "/workspace/out/staff_qa.md"}

# ACIA comment letter: GAAIA discussion draft

**American Compute & Innovation Alliance**
Washington, DC

[Date on send]

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
United States House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

The Honorable Lori Trahan
United States House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

Sent via GAAIA@mail.house.gov

**RE: ACIA comments on the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act**

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan:

Thank you for releasing the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act and for keeping the comment channel open ahead of introduction. The American Compute & Innovation Alliance is a coalition of roughly 140 member companies: AI developers, cloud and data-center operators, semiconductor startups, and venture firms. Our members build the models, chips, and data centers that will determine whether the United States leads in artificial intelligence or licenses it from someone else.

We write with one strong support, two strong objections, and support for most of the rest of the draft.

We support Sec. 121, which federalizes state regulation of AI model development. We ask you to make it permanent.

We ask you to strike the critical safety incident reporting provisions in Sec. 111(f) and (g), and the codification of the Center for AI Standards and Innovation in Sec. 102, including the $100 million annual authorization in Sec. 102(e). Both provisions write speculative doomsday scenarios into federal law. Neither would make anyone safer.

We can work with the balance of the draft. Section 6 of this letter lists the provisions we would support and fund.

## 1. Compliance costs are the industry's top federal AI problem

ACIA surveyed its members in August 2026. Eighty-six companies responded. The figures below are aggregate, and the sample is not a probability sample. The findings are consistent and, for a young industry, sobering.

- The median one-off cost of standing up an incident-reporting function was $310,000, with a middle range of $140,000 to $720,000.
- Developers subject to both California SB 53 and the New York RAISE Act report a median of 6.5 full-time employees just to run the two regimes side by side.
- Thirty-four percent of our startup members said they had delayed a launch in California or New York in the previous 12 months because of state AI rules.
- Sixty-one percent named conflicting state definitions as their single largest compliance problem.

Sec. 121 is the only provision that answers those numbers directly. The December 2025 executive order on a national AI policy framework created the Justice Department's AI Litigation Task Force and directed a Commerce review of state AI laws. The White House legislative framework of March 20, 2026 asked Congress to preempt state AI laws that impose undue burdens. Both are useful. Neither binds the states. Only a statute does.

## 2. Sec. 121: support, and make it permanent

The case for one national standard is already made. California's Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act has been in force since Jan. 1, 2026. New York's RAISE Act, as amended and signed March 27, takes effect Jan. 1, 2027 and adds a 72-hour incident clock plus a new oversight office inside the Department of Financial Services. Other states are queued up behind them. Our members do not ship different models to Sacramento and Buffalo, and they should not have to hire as though they do.

For our larger developers, maintaining a published frontier safety framework costs a median of $1.4 million a year. One standard, one template, and one set of definitions is worth real money to the companies that file against them.

The three-year sunset is the provision's central weakness, for three reasons.

First, it schedules the patchwork's return. Data centers, chip programs, and model roadmaps are planned in five-year increments. A standard that expires in 2027 or 2028 is not a standard; it is a grace period, and the state legislatures that passed SB 53 and the RAISE Act will simply wait it out.

Second, the draft's own architecture concedes the point. Sections 111 and 112 sunset at three years as well. In year four, the country would have neither a national standard nor the federal oversight regime the sponsors describe. Only the patchwork would remain, and it would come back with four years of pent-up state drafting behind it.

Third, the sunset would keep the lobbying war alive. Every affected stakeholder would spend the second and third years of the preemption period litigating its renewal rather than building.

**Requested changes:** Strike the sunset in Sec. 121 and make the federalization permanent. Confirm in text that Sec. 121 reaches the development-stage obligations in Sec. 111(a) through (c), so that the framework and transparency-report duties in SB 53 and the RAISE Act are actually frozen rather than merely restyled. And close the state attorney general opt-in that runs through Secs. 111 and 112. A national standard enforced by 50 state attorneys general is not one national standard.

## 3. Sec. 111(f) and (g): strike the incident-reporting mandate

Our members run real security programs, report real intrusions, and fix real defects. What we cannot support is a reporting mandate built on a premise the evidence does not support.

Look first at the definition. Sec. 101(7) defines a critical safety incident to include "a failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures" and "loss of control of such model." Neither is a harm. They are categories drawn from a specific theory of AI risk: that current systems might cause mass-casualty events or escape human control. There is no evidence that any current or foreseeable system can do either. Those scenarios come from thought experiments and contrived laboratory demonstrations, and the dangerous-capability and "scheming" studies cited in their support are lab setups that say nothing about real-world risk. Codifyi
... [1799 chars truncated] ...
k-publication and transparency-report obligations in Sec. 111(a) through (c), which mirror what large developers already publish under California law. Our objection is to the regulator-facing incident and enforcement machinery.

**Requested changes:** Strike Sec. 111(f)(1) and Sec. 111(g), along with the penalty hooks that depend on them. Keep the public transparency report, and harmonize its data elements with the California and New York reporting formats so that the preemption in Sec. 121 delivers an actual single standard.

## 4. Sec. 102: strike the CAISI codification and the $100 million

Sec. 102 would place the Center for AI Standards and Innovation in statute, license independent verification organizations through it, and authorize $100 million a year for fiscal 2027 through 2029, plus fee authority.

We ask you to strike it, and we will ask appropriators to zero out funding for CAISI and return NIST to its core measurement-science mission.

Three reasons.

First, this is an administrative experiment, not an institution. CAISI exists because the Commerce Secretary refashioned the U.S. AI Safety Institute into it in June 2025. Codifying that reorganization would freeze in place a body that has not yet demonstrated it needs to exist, and it would do so before the first audit has been conducted under Sec. 112.

Second, the money and the mandate do not match the mission. The sponsors' own frequently-asked-questions document puts CAISI's current appropriation at roughly $15 million. Sec. 102(e) would take that to $100 million a year, roughly sevenfold, and Sec. 102(f) adds fee authority charged to the verification organizations and large frontier developers. A federal center that is paid by the companies it polices, and that decides which auditors are allowed to judge those companies, is a textbook regulatory-capture risk. NIST's comparative advantage is measurement science: time, standards, benchmarks, and test methods. That is where the public gets value for money.

Third, the standards work the draft wants does not need a $100 million regulator-adjacent center. Our comments to the Office of Science and Technology Policy in March 2025 made the same point: keep standards voluntary and industry-led. The provisions we support below, including the testbeds in Sec. 401 and the international coalitions in Sec. 411, are the right vehicles.

**Requested changes:** Strike Sec. 102 in its entirety, including the authorization in Sec. 102(e) and the fee authority in Sec. 102(f), and make conforming changes to Secs. 111, 112, and 311, each of which currently routes work through the Center. We would support redirecting that budget authority to the testbed program and the National AI Research Resource.

## 5. The narrative behind Title I

We would not ask you to strike these provisions if they were merely redundant. They are also unwise, because they legislate a claim that has not been established.

The claim is that frontier models pose a catastrophic, loss-of-control risk requiring a standing federal reporting and audit apparatus. That claim is unfounded. It has been advanced by a small, well-funded advocacy network with outsized influence on Washington AI policy. Open Philanthropy, which now operates as Coefficient Giving, reported committing $351 million across its AI safety, security, and field-building portfolio in 2025 and expects to commit more than $1 billion this year. The vocabulary of that network is now the vocabulary of Secs. 101 and 111. Congress should legislate from evidence, not from a donor's theory of the future.

The administration has chosen a different register for the same concern. The White House Accord on Super Intelligence of Sept. 29 is a voluntary joint commitment, built on internal controls and review layers that companies can revise as the technology changes. That is the model our members can work inside: transparent, revisable in months rather than amendable only after years, and without a complaint docket feeding a federal center.

## 6. Provisions ACIA supports

We want to be useful on the rest of the draft, and we are. ACIA supports:

- **Sec. 401**, the AI testbed program at the Energy Department, NIST, and the National Science Foundation, including reproducible evaluations and hackathons.
- **Sec. 423**, codification of the National AI Research Resource.
- **Sec. 311**, grants to maintainers of critical open-source software. We ask only that the model-access condition be developed with developers so it does not become a security liability.
- **Sec. 411**, international standards coalitions that promote private-sector-led, U.S.-developed standards and counter foreign adversary influence in standards bodies.
- **Sec. 301**, reauthorization of the Cybersecurity Act of 2015, which lets companies share threat information without antitrust exposure.
- **Secs. 131 and 132**, higher penalties for AI-enabled fraud and for impersonation of federal officials.
- **Sec. 122**, the GAO report on regulatory impediments to AI innovation, and **Sec. 321**, the report on model-weight, data center, and open-source security.
- **Sec. 141**, the study of government pressure on AI platforms.

## 7. A word on H.R. 9925

The transparency, audit, and incident-reporting architecture at issue here now also exists as introduced legislation, in the FRONTIER Act, H.R. 9925, which you introduced on July 23 with your four co-sponsors from the discussion draft. Our comments above apply to that bill with equal force. We would welcome the chance to work with your staffs on both.

Thank you for the genuinely bipartisan effort this draft represents. Preemption done properly is the single highest-value thing Congress can do for the American AI industry this year, and we would like to help you do it properly.

Respectfully,

**Grant Holloway**
President & CEO
American Compute & Innovation Alliance

Contact: Tessa Marchetti, Vice President for Policy, ACIA. [Email and phone to be inserted on send.]

# ACIA asks by section: GAAIA discussion draft

Positions per the ACIA messaging guide v4 (board-approved Sept. 30, 2026). Section numbers confirmed against the sponsors' discussion draft text and section-by-section summary. Contact: Tessa Marchetti, VP Policy.

| Draft provision | Our position | Requested change | One-line rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sec. 101(7), definitions ("critical safety incident") | Oppose | Delete "a failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures" and "loss of control of such model" from the definition | These describe a scenario for which there is no evidence, and they would make lab findings and red-team results federally reportable events. |
| Sec. 101, definitions ("catastrophic risk," "frontier AI framework") | Oppose as the draft's organizing concept | Do not key any Title I obligation to "catastrophic risk"; conform definitions to whatever duties survive | The draft's whole oversight structure is built on a risk narrative drawn from thought experiments and contrived lab demonstrations. |
| Sec. 102, CAISI codification | Strike | Strike Sec. 102; make conforming changes in Secs. 111, 112 and 311, which route work through the Center | Codifying a 2025 administrative reorganization locks in a body that has yet to prove a statutory mission. |
| Sec. 102(e), $100 million annual authorization, FY2027-2029 | Strike | Strike the authorization; urge appropriators to zero out CAISI funding | Roughly seven times the Center's current appropriation, for a standards body, not a regulator. |
| Sec. 102(f), fee authority charged to IVOs and large frontier developers | Strike | Strike fee authority | A center paid by the companies it polices invites regulatory capture. |
| Sec. 111(a)-(c), frontier AI framework and transparency reports | No objection | Harmonize report data elements with California and New York formats | These mirror obligations our larger members already publish; a single template is where preemption pays off. |
| Sec. 111(f)(1), federal incident-reporting mechanism, public complaints | Strike | Strike the mechanism and the 180-day build requirement | A channel open to any member of the public, keyed to an elastic definition, is a complaint docket, not a safety system. |
| Sec. 111(g), 15-day and 24-hour reporting clocks | Strike | Strike both clocks | The real-world analogue is a cyber intrusion, and CISA's CIRCIA rule already sets the federal reporting timeline. |
| Secs. 111 and 112, penalties up to $1 million per day; state AG opt-in | Strike | Strike the penalty and opt-in provisions with the mandates they enforce | Fifty state attorneys general enforcing one federal standard is not one national standard. |
| Sec. 112, CAISI-licensed independent verification organizations | Strike | Strike the IVO licensing and semi-annual audit regime | Mandatory audits of "acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation" rest on the same unfounded premise as Sec. 111. |
| Sec. 113, whistleblower protections | No position | None | Our objection is to the reporting and audit mandates, not to protections against retaliation. |
| Sec. 121, federalization of state AI development laws | Support, strengthen | Strike the three-year sunset; confirm coverage of Sec. 111(a)-(c) duties; close the state AG opt-in | The patchwork is the industry's top cost driver, and a sunsetted standard is a grace period. |
| Sec. 122, GAO report on regulatory impediments to AI innovation | Support | None | A useful inventory of federal barriers, including energy. |
| Secs. 131-132, AI-enabled fraud and impersonation penalties | Support | None | Penalties tied to real, demonstrated harms are the right model. |
| Sec. 141, study of government pressure on AI platforms | Support | None | Jawboning deserves a documented record. |
| Sec. 301, Cybersecurity Act of 2015 reauthorization | Support | None | Threat information sharing without antitrust exposure helps our operators. |
| Sec. 311, grants for critical open-source software maintainers | Support, amend | Keep the grants; write the model-access condition with developers so it does not become a security liability | Funding maintainers is good hygiene; mandating access needs care. |
| Sec. 321, report on model-weight, data center and open-source security | Support | None | Useful facts on the security issues that actually matter. |
| Sec. 401, AI testbed program at DOE, NIST and NSF | Support, fund | Fund it with dollars redirected from the CAISI authorization | Reproducible evaluation at the labs is measurement science, which is NIST's job. |
| Sec. 411, international AI standards coalitions | Support | None | Private-sector-led, U.S.-developed standards, with adversary influence countered. |
| Sec. 423, National AI Research Resource codification | Support | None | Compute access for researchers and startups widens the frontier beyond a handful of labs. |

## 3. Sec. 111(f) and (g): strike the incident-reporting mandate

Our members run real security programs, report real intrusions, and fix real defects. What we cannot support is a reporting mandate built on a premise the evidence does not support.

Look first at the definition. Sec. 101(7) defines a critical safety incident to include "a failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures" and "loss of control of such model." Neither is a harm. They are categories drawn from a specific theory of AI risk: that current systems might cause mass-casualty events or escape human control. There is no evidence that any current or foreseeable system can do either. Those scenarios come from thought experiments and contrived laboratory demonstrations, and the dangerous-capability and "scheming" studies cited in their support are lab setups that say nothing about real-world risk. Codifying that vocabulary in Sec. 101 does not make it true, but it does make it binding.

The design problems follow from the definition. Sec. 111(f)(1) directs the Director to stand up a mechanism, within 180 days of enactment, for "a frontier developer or member of the public" to report critical safety incidents. A reporting channel open to any member of the public, keyed to a term as elastic as "a failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures," is a complaint docket, not a safety system. It will be fed by activists and competitors, and it will be litigated. Sec. 111(g) then sets a 15-day clock on all incidents and a 24-hour clock where there is an imminent risk of death or serious physical injury, with penalties of up to $1 million per day per violation and an opt-in for state attorneys general.

Second, the mandate is duplicative. The real-world analogue of an AI incident is an intrusion, and federal law already handles intrusions. The Cyber Incident Reporting for Critical Infrastructure Act rule, which CISA sent to the Office of Management and Budget for review on Oct. 1, will require covered critical-infrastructure entities to report covered cyber incidents within 72 hours and ransom payments within 24 hours. Unauthorized access to or exfiltration of model weights is a cyber incident. Where it matters, it is already reported.

Third, the mandate re-creates at the federal level exactly what Sec. 121 is meant to displace. Our members would spend a median of $310,000 to stand up the function, and the developers now running SB 53 and RAISE programs would carry their state reporting staff over to a federal one. Trading 50 mandates for one federal mandate is not the deal our members are asking for.

To be clear about what we are not asking: we take no issue with the framework-publication and transparency-report obligations in Sec. 111(a) through (c), which mirror what large developers already publish under California law. Our objection is to the regulator-facing incident and enforcement machinery.

**Requested changes:** Strike Sec. 111(f)(1) and Sec. 111(g), along with the penalty hooks that depend on them. Keep the public transparency report, and harmonize its data elements with the California and New York reporting formats so that the preemption in Sec. 121 delivers an actual single standard.

## 4. Sec. 102: strike the CAISI codification and the $100 million
